newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks rebound, lifted by bargain hunters.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks rebound, lifted by bargain hunters.

text.p: Tokyo stocks rebounded on Wednesday and broke a three-session losing streak, lifted by bargain hunting in the banking sector and investor interest in certain semiconductor-related issues, brokers said.
The Nikkei 225 ended 187.62 points or 0.96 percent higher at 19,702.07. September Nikkei futures added 310 to 19,750.

"There were newspaper reports about chip equipment makers boosting output and the lifting of a ban on perpetual bonds, and this buoyed the market," said Akihiro Naemura, Okasan Securities general manager.
"But despite the reports, the market was slow to respond, and the response itself was not as strong as it could have been which means the rise today was mostly technical," Naemura added.

Losers beat winners 586 to 521 -- further proof that the market was not on a solid recovery track -- while 152 issues were unchanged. Turnover was 392 million yen compared to 429 million on the previous day.
The most heavily traded issue was Daiwa Bank Ltd, with 5.79 million shares traded. It ended up 13 yen at 573.

Short covering of bank issues was sparked by a financial daily report saying that the Finance and Justice Ministries had agreed to lift the ban on perpetual bonds, which will help banks improve their capital adequacy ratios.
Ministry officials were not available for comment.
Shares of Nikon Corp, a major camera maker that also produces semiconductor-related equipment, rose 150 yen to a record high of 2,270.
The Nihon Kezai Shimbun said Japanese chip equipment firms were increasing output to meet expanding demand from U.S. and Taiwanese chip makers.
"High-techs are slowing but Nikon is bucking the trend," a trader at a second-tier brokerage said. "Nikon's PER is over 100 times and it is not a bargain, so the rise today was supported by demand."
The stock market largely shrugged off Japan's customs-cleared trade data for the first 20 days of July which showed the surplus up 126.4 percent year on year.
But the dollar which stood at around 119 yen to the yen, up from about 118 yen in late Tokyo trade on Tuesday helped investors bargain hunt for battered automobile sector issues.
Toyota Motor Corp rose 100 yen to 3,260.
Brokers said that there was still a lot of apprehension about growth in the car sector, and that the buying may not last as recent data showed domestic sales had not picked up.

"Uncertainty over the recovery of the economy is casting a pall over the market and investors have no choice but to seek a safe-haven in blue chips," said Tadahiro Kamogawa, Yamaichi Securities general manager.
He added that the bargain-hunting zone is anywhere below the 19,500 line.
Market participants reacted calmly to the partial business suspension of Nomura Securities Co Ltd.

"The penalties would have a negative influence on the stock market's overall volume, but the share price rose, supported by Nomura's evaluation for the long term," Tokyo Securities general manager Kunihiro Hatae said.
Nomura shares were up 50 yen at 1,680

Brokers said that there was a chance that volatility could increase during Nomura's absence, as smaller brokerages, with less stock on hand, handling large orders from investors may need to rely on margin transactions to meet demand.
"With market activity as thin as it is, if margin trading increases, indices could move sharply," one broker said.

Real estate, precision, instruments, banks, automobiles and pharmaceuticals topped the list of advancing sectors. Transport equipment, oil, iron/steel, warehouses and textiles were the top retreaters.

The bank-studded TOPIX index added 20.50 points or 1.38 percent to end at 1,507.63. The Nikkei 300 climbed 4.77 points or 1.64 percent to 294.83. The second section index fell 6.64 points or 0.39 percent to end at 1,708.29.
The over-the-counter index was down 4.43 points or 0.40 percent at 1,095.67 in late trade.
-- Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk +81-3-3432-9052
